1.pericope_label: Therefore thus saith the Lord God; Behold, I am against thee, O Tyrus, and will cause many nations to come up against thee, as the sea causeth his waves to come up
debates: Whether the many nations are one mixed army or successive conquests
Whether the desolation was fulfilled by Nebuchadnezzar
Which month the oracle belongs to
outliers: Clarke doubts that the many nations are the mixed provinces of the Chaldean army and prefers the successive nations that fought Tyre in later ages, down to the sixteenth century
Clarke holds the scraping of the dust cannot refer to the capture by Nebuchadnezzar, since the city flourished long after his time
Ellicott says the month cannot now be ascertained and treats the Greek supplement of the first month as a conjecture, the omission being probably a scribal error
Henry distinguishes the motive of Tyre from that of the Ammonites and Edomites, calling it commercial rivalry rather than religious hatred
themes: Fishermen drying nets on stones made smooth by sun and wave
A city treated as a rival rather than an enemy
Two cities, one taken quickly and one after thirteen years, forming a single state
Ruins thrown into the sea and replaced by later ones

7.pericope_label: And I will make thee like the top of a rock: thou shalt be a place to spread nets upon; thou shalt be built no more
debates: Which conquest of Tyre the passage describes
How a mainland siege could be laid against an island
outliers: Clarke takes the casting of stones into the sea as answering to the work of Alexander, and doubts the whole prophecy refers to the capture by Nebuchadnezzar
Ellicott finds the same widening in the grammar, the nominative changing from Nebuchadnezzar to they at the twelfth verse
Ellicott corrects strong garrisons to the pillars of thy strength, probably the two pillars an ancient historian saw in the temple at Tyre
Wesley meets the difficulty of a later Tyre by observing that it was built on the continent and in propriety of speech was another city
themes: A channel of twelve hundred yards crossed by a bridge of boats
A mole that silted until an island became a peninsula
Marble columns counted lying under the water
Booty said to be small because the wealth went out by sea

15.pericope_label: I will make thee a terror, and thou shalt be no more: though thou be sought for, yet shalt thou never be found again, saith the Lord God
debates: Whether the oracle forbids any later habitation on the rock
What inhabited of seafaring men means
outliers: Ellicott holds that isles covers any sea-coast, and lists the Phoenician colonies that looked to Tyre as their mother city
Ellicott expressly limits the vision to the Tyre that then was, saying the question of later inhabitants on the rock does not come within its scope at all
Clarke by contrast extends the prophecy over the entire duration of Tyre, while recording honestly that it was a place of some consequence long afterwards
Ellicott corrects inhabited of seafaring men to inhabited from the sea, the word never meaning men
themes: A Tyrian respected abroad as a Roman later was for the sake of Rome
Colonies sending yearly presents to their mother city
Seven months spent filling an arm of the sea
Language about the dead defended as a necessity of human thought
